comparison: Both strongly support the core finding that Vif causes pseudo-metaphase arrest rather than G2 arrest (C4-C7). OpenEval emphasizes the contradiction with prior assumptions and comprehensive live-cell imaging evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this finding as 'convincing' and 'elegant,' with one noting the distinction from flow cytometry-based G2 arrest characterizations. Both also reference the distinction between Vif and Vpr effects (C33-C41, C42-C50, C52-C54 in peer R1).

Both support the live-cell imaging data showing quantitative differences in mitotic duration and cell fate outcomes between Vif, Vpr, and Vif+Vpr conditions (C33-C41). OpenEval notes adequate sample sizes and statistical significance. Peer reviewers affirm the authors 'convincingly show a difference between Vif and Vpr-mediated cell cycle arrests.'

Both support the live-cell imaging evidence for pseudo-metaphase arrest across multiple cell lines (C42-C50). OpenEval emphasizes the distinction from typical prometaphase arrest and corroboration with fixed immunofluorescence. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall pseudo-metaphase phenotype characterization.

Both support the sufficiency experiments showing Vif alone induces arrest (C52-C54). OpenEval highlights the conditional expression experiments eliminating confounding effects from other viral proteins. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their affirmation of the overall Vif-specific pseudo-metaphase arrest phenotype.

Both support the cell cycle phase duration findings (C55-C58). OpenEval notes the novel single-cell tracking method and contradiction with prior G2/M arrest assumptions. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings, which support the conclusion that Vif acts specifically during mitosis rather than earlier phases.

Both support the p53-independence findings (C59-C64). OpenEval emphasizes the use of matched wild-type and p53 KO cell lines directly contradicting prior work (C26). Peer reviewers do not question these results, implicitly accepting them through their overall acceptance of the pseudo-metaphase arrest phenotype.

Both support the chromosome distribution and oscillation findings (C65-C69). OpenEval highlights super-resolution and live-cell imaging evidence with near-complete penetrance. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'chromosome segregation is dysregulated' and note the correlation with 'impaired assembly of microtubules at the kinetochore.'

Both support the spindle multi-polarity and dynamics findings (C70-C75). OpenEval explains the discrepancy between fixed and live imaging frequencies due to temporal dynamics. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall dysregulation of chromosome segregation and kinetochore function.

Both support the PP2A-B56 depletion at kinetochores (C79-C83). OpenEval emphasizes the nocodazole control experiment and adequate sample size. Peer reviewers explicitly support this, with one stating the authors 'make a strong case for this phenotype being tied to the degradation of PP2-B56 by Vif.' One reviewer initially questioned whether kinetochore-specific reduction was distinct from general cellular degradation, but notes this was clarified in revision. Peer R5 also includes C8 and C10 not in OpenEval R8.

Both support the Plk1 dysregulation findings (C87-C91). OpenEval notes Plk1 serves as a functional readout validating B56 depletion and strengthens the mechanistic link. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings, implicitly accepting them as consistent with PP2A-B56 loss and the overall mechanistic model.

Both support the Astrin-SKAP complex disruption and PP1 reduction at kinetochores (C95-C101). OpenEval emphasizes the sister kinetochore imbalance analysis revealing force imbalances. Peer reviewers explicitly accept the 'lack of recruitment of B56-subunits' and the mechanistic connection to PP1 recruitment as part of the accepted model.

Both support the Hec1 hyperphosphorylation findings (C103-C108). OpenEval highlights this as direct functional evidence for reduced PP1 activity at kinetochores. Peer reviewers do not challenge these results, accepting them as mechanistically consistent with disrupted Astrin-PP1 complex assembly and supporting the model of impaired kinetochore-microtubule interactions.

Both support the integrative conclusions linking reduced Astrin-PP1, elevated Hec1 phosphorylation, and force imbalances (C109-C110). OpenEval notes this provides molecular explanation for chromosome oscillations. Peer reviewers accept this interpretation, with one noting it 'weakens and unbalances the microtubule-mediated forces on the separating chromosomes.'

Both support the overall mechanistic model (C115-C122). OpenEval notes the model integrates all experimental findings and is consistent with established cell cycle biology, though largely inferential. Peer reviewers explicitly support this interpretation, with one stating the authors 'make a strong case for this phenotype being tied to the degradation of PP2-B56 by Vif' and the editor confirming findings 'could be explained by the loss of phosphatase functions.'

Both support the finding that C-terminal tagged Vif constructs fail to induce arrest (C51). OpenEval notes this is an important methodological finding explaining why direct Vif localization visualization was not possible. Peer reviewers do not challenge this technical observation, which is consistent with known Vif functional requirements.

Both address methodological choices (C123-C127). OpenEval finds the rationale for cell line choice and viral construct design sound and appropriate for isolating Vif effects, though noting limited direct relevance to full viral infection. Peer reviewers raise a major concern about the relevance of tumor cell lines to actual HIV-1 infections in primary T cells, noting 'none of these cells are relevant targets and tumor cells have different cell death and cell cycle regulation.' While authors acknowledged this caveat in revision, the fundamental limitation remains. This represents a significant divergence in evaluation.

OpenEval supports background claims about Vif function and APOBEC3 counteraction (C1-C2, C21-C24) as well-supported by literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background claims.

OpenEval supports prior literature claims about Vif's cell cycle effects (C3, C25-C27, C30), noting they establish the knowledge gap addressed by the study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background claims.

OpenEval supports numerous background claims about cell cycle biology (C76-C78, C80, C84-C86, C92-C94, C102, C111-C114, C119, C121) as established knowledge with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background claims, though peer R9 overlaps with C119 and C121 in the context of the mechanistic model.
OpenEval supports background claims about HIV-1 biology (C11-C20) as accurate and well-cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background claims.
OpenEval supports background claims about cell cycle regulators (C28-C29, C31-C32) with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific background claims.

OpenEval supports the claim distinguishing Vif-induced arrest from typical mitotic inhibitors (C44), noting it strengthens the novelty of the pseudo-metaphase phenotype. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim.

OpenEval supports the background claim about Vpr (C36), noting the current study reveals Vpr actually induces mild prometaphase arrest (C37). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific background claim.
